resolution.comment: The note and locus are now December 522. I re-read Chron. Edessa 89-90 (cowper lines 221, 223). Paul is sent to Euchata and leaves on 27 Tammuz 833 (July 522). Asclepius enters on 23 Tishri I 834 (October 522). The expulsion falls in Canun I after that, so December 522. Seleucid 834 runs from October 522, so the conversion holds. 'Removed in 522' is fair: the attempt began in 519, but he left in July 522. The two new section 89 quotes show Paul refusing 'the synod', which section 88 identifies as including Chalcedon.

The note now claims only that the see of Nisibis continued. The Chronicle names Jacob (line 77, An. 649 = 337/8) and Vologesh (line 91, same year as s. 23, An. 672 = 360/1) as bishops of Nisibis. Osee signs at 410 and is named second metropolitan (Synodicon 17861, 17745-17746). The see therefore appears on both sides of 363, which is the round-1 condition for Documented. The brief accepts see continuity for 'continued as'. The date 363 is sourced to Gwynn (npnf213 12207-12208), and Ephrem's withdrawal to Barhadbeshabba. The 'daughter' sentence and Wigram are gone. Dropping 'its church passed with it' is right. Gwynn at npnf213 10833 reports the city 'emptied of its Christian inhabitants', so the note now claims nothing the evidence contradicts.

Wigram is dropped, and the link is regraded Inferential-Thin. The note says plainly that 'these few notices are thin evidence for a line of descent'. Menze and Frend are in wants. The reviser also dropped the bishop-list sentence and Rabbula, which leaves the note with no bridge from the 200-410 movement. That makes it a little thinner, but it is still accurate and still honest about being thin. It is not a substantial finding.

The new sentence names Victorinus as this church's bishop. It says only that he wrote on the Apocalypse and that Jerome reissued the book with a new ending. The movement's own text supports that ('revised the Apocalypse commentary'; 'rewrote the ending'). The reviser declined 'first bishop-writer' because nothing supports it, which is sound. The referent problem is fixed. FRE 61.0, FK 8.5.

All six named paragraphs are re-joined. I re-scored every changed paragraph with engine.m7.turn_readability.score_turn: manichaeism longDescription 62.2/8.5, why 65.7/8.4; marcion why 65.1/9.2; antiochene longDescription 62.5/9.1; post-apostolic legacy 68.7/8.9; anatolian why 60.7/7.4. Facts were kept, and the primer-style runs are gone in these paragraphs. The reviser says FK 7.4-7.6 is the ceiling where FRE sits at 60.6-60.7. That fits the scores: those paragraphs have no FRE headroom. One new paragraph from the follow-up repeats the pattern; see R2-03.
'Sometimes' is restored, and 'taking the good and leaving the bad' is added. A second quote, npnf206 15123-15124, carries it, and in context it covers Tertullian among the writers Jerome lists.
The sentence 'The dialogues themselves are lost' is dropped. The Greek translation now has its own quote (26638-26639). In context the subject is 'His pupils' on 26637.

The reviser added sources rather than replacing them. VI.24.3 'He wrote also the books De Principiis' (36069) now names the work. McGiffert's note at 36070-36071 ('written before he left Alexandria') is a secondary source with a file, and it carries 'written at Alexandria' more exactly than the chapter title. Keeping the title as well does no harm.

The first quote is removed. The reviser kept Apolinarius with post-apostolic-house-church on purpose. The reason given is sound: an Asian bishop writing against a movement in his own region, which Eusebius places after the apology ('subsequently', npnf201 26112). The Anonymous quote at anf07 11308 continues 'expelled from the Church and debarred from communion', which supports 'cut its followers off from communion'.

The Aurelian sentence and its quote are dropped. The reason is correct: c. 272 falls after roman-church-third-century ends in 268. The letter to Dionysius alone carries the contact. The antiochene longDescription still tells the Aurelian story as narrative, which needs no link.

Eusebius VII.28 and Origen X.17 keep their fragments, and the work fields now say that an editor's footnote splits each clause, as the brief allows. The Trullo quote is now one clause-bounded list item (26742-26745). For Ambrose, the reviser's reading of the validator is correct (tools/validate-census.mjs squashes whitespace and does not strip tags). But the remedy left a five-word fragment, and the new DVI 83 quote keeps its markup anyway; see R2-01.

'Writing at Rome' is dropped. 'Around 400' is kept and cited to the NPNF 1.4 heading 'Written about the year 400.' (npnf104 4292), entered as a secondary source with a file. That is a listed source. The extended quote at 4308 carries 'he had once met'.

The rhetorical question is gone, and paragraph 3 reads 'later remembered the school in two minds'. The reviser changed 'not schooled in the city' to 'a boy who would not learn letters'. That is closer to VA 1 ('could not endure to learn letters', npnf204 31221) and does not settle the literacy question, so the change is sound. It does leave 'letters' in two senses in adjacent sentences; see R2-06.
All three stock lines are replaced as proposed. 'All the others the movement wrote' is the same claim as 'every other line the movement produced'.

The new 'influenced' link is graded Documented on Jerome DVI 83 (npnf203 41096-41098), which lists the 'Banquet of the ten virgins' among Methodius's works. Under the brief, the later side naming the earlier side's work documents 'influenced'. The note claims naming only. The dates fit: DVI was written in the 390s, inside hieronymian's 382-420, and Methodius falls in anatolian's 240-312.

greek-apologists longDescription now says 'He also attacked Marcion and the Valentinians, whom he called Christians in name only.' This is supported by Dial. 35 ('confessors of Jesus in name only'; 'Some are called Marcians, and some Valentinians', anf01 19250-19255) and 1 Apol. 26. The reviser declined 'refused to call Christians' because Justin says they 'style themselves Christians', which is the more accurate reading. FRE 63.1, FK 7.5.
See R1-15.

The reviser reworded rather than adding a Wigram 'gave rise to' link. That is sound: a second link on the same pair, saying 'emerged from' alongside 'same see', would rest on one 1910 author. The follow-up states the Syriac Orthodox side as that church's own claim ('counts it as a root'), which matches the Inferential-Thin link. 'Syriac translators' fixes the referent of 'Their'. The follow-up's legacy rewrite raises a new minor point; see R2-03.

The new link imperial-juridical-christianity--ebionite-nazoraean-current is drafted, and the mapping is sound. First, imperial-juridical's own voices name 'Eusebius of Caesarea [who] wrote the first history of the church'. Second, the census already maps the writing of the Church History to imperial-juridical in palestinian-church-pre-constantinian--imperial-juridical-christianity ('drew material for his Church History from the library at Aelia'), so this mapping is consistent with it. Third, McGiffert dates completion to 324 (widest limits late 323 to early 325), inside 312-451. The reviser honestly discloses McGiffert's caveat that the earlier books were 'at least completed long before' (npnf201 4573-4606, with the first nine books after the edict of Milan). The note therefore dates only the finished work, which avoids the problem. The palestinian movement's legacy also claims the History, but as a product of its library, not as the movement writing against anyone. That is no conflict. Type, arrow and Documented grade are right: HE III.27.1 is a text directed at the Ebionites by name ('brought them over to his own purposes'; 'poor and mean opinions concerning Christ', 18512-18516). One quote boundary is minor; see R2-02.

'Augustine called his many works eloquent and still read' matches De haer. 86 on the existing link. The full readability pass on that paragraph (38.1 -> 67.6, FK 7.7) keeps every fact. 'Legal terms' and 'never made a saint' are plain equivalents of the old words. 'He gave Latin its words for the Trinity' says no more than the old 'his legacy is ... the Latin words for the Trinity'.

The disposition, a no-entry gap, is agreed. But the Open_Gaps_Tracking entry is not written. A repo-wide search finds no Irenaeus no-entry entry, and none for escalation items D (Montanism end date) and B (raw ids in four era-2+ movements). The reviser was right not to write it, since only one output file was allowed. The caller has to log it; see R2-04.

findings.issue: To avoid italic markup, the quote was cut to 'Recently also Ambrose appropriated his'. That fragment ends on a possessive and does not show what was taken, so it is a worse fragment than before. In the same pass the new DVI 83 quote keeps its '<i>' markup, so the two quotes now follow inconsistent rules. The link still holds: the second quote names Origen, and the context shows the relationship.
findings.evidence: npnf206 19268-19269 raw: 'Recently also Ambrose appropriated his Six\nDays’ Work,Six Days’ Work,' passed the validator. The DVI 83 quote at npnf203 41096-41098 keeps ''.
findings.fix: Restore the round-1 quote 'Recently also Ambrose appropriated his Six Days’ Work,' (lines 19268-19269), and say in the work field that the title is in italic markup, as is already done for DVI 83. The site-side rendering flag from R1-11 then covers both.

findings.issue: The quote that carries 'around 324' starts mid-sentence at 'or, to give the widest possible limits' and does not contain the year 324. The work field has to supply it.
findings.evidence: npnf201 4569-4571: 'We are thus led to place the completion of the History in the year 324, or, to give the widest possible limits, between the latter part of 323 and the early part of 325 a.d.'
findings.fix: Quote the whole sentence at lines 4569-4571, from 'We are thus led' to '325 a.d.' (31 words; check that the validator matches the small-caps 'a.d.' span, or end at '325'). Then shorten the work field.

findings.issue: Two problems. First, the new opening 'Three groups of churches still worship in Syriac. They are ...' presents the list as complete. The old text made no such claim; it only said these three worship in Syriac, and no source here shows the list is exhaustive. Second, the rewrite reintroduces the primer-style split that R1-05 removed elsewhere ('They are the ...'), at FK 6.6. It also repeats 'worship' ('worship in Syriac ... in their own worship'). The softening to 'each counts this tradition as a root' is justified by the reason given.
findings.evidence: score_turn: FRE 75.4, FK 6.6. Old text: 'The Assyrian Church of the East, the Syriac Orthodox Church, and the Eastern Catholic churches in communion with Rome all descend from this tradition, still worship in Syriac, and still sing Ephrem's hymns in their own liturgies.'
findings.fix: 'Syriac is still a language of worship in the Assyrian Church of the East, the Syriac Orthodox Church, and the Eastern Catholic churches in union with Rome. All of them still sing Ephrem's hymns, and each counts this tradition as a root.' (score_turn: FRE 68.7, FK 8.9.)

findings.issue: 'Antony's letters' and 'would not learn letters' sit in adjacent sentences, with 'letters' in two senses. For a B2 reader the contrast reads as wordplay, or as confusion. The source wording is right, and the meaning is right.
findings.evidence: New text: 'One modern reading finds Origen's ideas in Antony's letters. But Athanasius shows him as a boy raised at home by Christian parents, a boy who would not learn letters.' VA 1: 'could not endure to learn letters' (npnf204 31221).
findings.fix: Optional: 'a boy who would not be taught to read'. That keeps VA 1's sense and settles nothing about the adult Antony. Re-score it; this paragraph sits at FRE 63.5.
